Schools and movements

Cognitive neuroscience

How the brain makes memory, attention and language possible.

What does it propose?Mental processes can be studied both in behaviour and in the brain, and each level helps us understand the other.
What does it study?The brain bases of perception, attention, memory, language, emotion and decision-making.
How does it study it?Studies of patients with lesions, electroencephalography, functional magnetic resonance imaging, transcranial magnetic stimulation and computational models.
Who took part?Michael Gazzaniga and George Miller, who coined the name in the late 1970s; Brenda Milner, Endel Tulving, Michael Posner, Marcus Raichle, Nancy Kanwisher, Eleanor Maguire.
What remains?A far more detailed map of how the brain is organised, the study of plasticity and applications in neurology, rehabilitation and diagnosis.
What is debated?The risk of 'neuro-allure': striking images that seem to explain more than they do. Many studies used small samples, and locating a function is not enough to understand it.

Context

For much of the twentieth century, cognitive psychology studied the mind without looking at the brain, and neurology studied the brain without asking much about the mind. In the late 1970s Michael Gazzaniga and George Miller used the name "cognitive neuroscience", in a New York taxi according to Gazzaniga, to describe the field they wanted to create.

The technique that changed the field arrived in 1990–1992: functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in oxygenated blood flow and shows which areas become active during a task without opening the skull.

What it has contributed

  • Confirmation that memory is not a single system, as the case of H. M., studied by Brenda Milner, had already suggested.
  • The discovery of specialised regions, such as the fusiform face area described by Nancy Kanwisher in 1997.
  • The "default mode network", active when we are not doing any specific task, described by Marcus Raichle in 2001.
  • Evidence of plasticity in adults, such as the hippocampus of London taxi drivers.

Limits

In 2009 a study with a dead salmon showed "activation" in fMRI when statistical analyses were not properly corrected, a warning about methodology. Today larger samples are used, data are shared and researchers stress that the brain works in networks, not in isolated "centres".

Tools, each with its limits

  • Electroencephalography: measures electrical activity with great temporal precision, in milliseconds, but localises poorly.
  • Functional MRI: localises well but is slow, because it measures blood flow, which takes a few seconds.
  • Transcranial magnetic stimulation: briefly disrupts an area to see which function is affected, allowing causal inference.

Neuromyths

The popularity of neuroscience has brought myths: that we use 10% of the brain, that there are left- or right-brained people, or that "learning styles" have a brain basis. Surveys of teachers in several countries show that many believe them. A 2008 study found that adding irrelevant neuroscience made people rate bad explanations more highly.

It takes thousands of brains

For years, many neuroimaging studies linked traits such as intelligence or depression to differences in the brain using a few dozen people. In 2022, Scott Marek and colleagues analysed data from around 50,000 people and showed that, for questions of this kind, the real effects are small and thousands of participants are needed to detect them reliably. With small samples, striking results are often flukes. Today work increasingly uses large shared datasets such as UK Biobank.

Reading the brain to restore a voice

Brain–computer interfaces record the activity of neurons in the motor cortex and translate it into commands. In 2021, a man with paralysis wrote about 90 characters a minute by imagining handwriting. In 2023, two US teams enabled people who had lost speech through ALS or stroke to produce text from their attempts to speak, at more than 60 words a minute. These are still experimental systems, but they show what cognitive neuroscience can contribute to rehabilitation.

Libet and free will

In 1983, Benjamin Libet asked volunteers to move their hand whenever they wished and to report when they had felt the intention to do so. Movement-related brain activity began about 350 milliseconds before people noticed that intention. Many took this as proof that free will is an illusion. Later analyses, such as Aaron Schurger's in 2012, suggest the signal reflects background fluctuations that make movement easier rather than a decision already made. The philosophical debate continues, but the experiment shows less than was claimed.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.
